A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. The main theoretical sections and Appendices A-C can be matched reliably, and the text, equations, figures, tables, and added experimental material are readable.

before.justification: v1.pdf contains theoretical results, proofs, and analytical regression and topic-classification examples. Inspection of the main text and appendices establishes no original experimental or simulation outcomes.

after.justification: Section 6 reports original synthetic regression experiments in Figure 1. Appendix D reports original CLIP training and ImageNet-1k zero-shot classification results in Table 1.

M1.justification: The proposed SimCLR/InfoNCE and chi-squared objectives and learning procedures in Equations (3) and (10) are retained. The new experiments instantiate these existing losses with neural-network encoders and selected link functions; they do not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluation on synthetic Gaussian regression and on image-text pretraining using 100,000 cc3m-wds pairs followed by ImageNet-1k zero-shot classification. v1's regression and topic-classification examples are analytical, so these constitute substantial new empirical coverage.

E2.justification: v2 introduces evaluated comparisons among InfoNCE, chi-squared contrastive learning, and Direct LR in Figure 1, and between InfoNCE and chi-squared learning in Table 1. v1 discusses these approaches and compares regression estimators theoretically, but reports no empirical comparator results.

E3.justification: Two experimental protocols are added. Synthetic pretraining uses 500 samples, batch size 64, and 1,000 epochs, followed by excess-risk evaluation across downstream sample sizes 150-10,000. CLIP uses 32 epochs, batch size 128, learning-rate selection, and zero-shot top-5 accuracy. These are new protocols, not revisions to previously reported experiments.

E4.justification: Figure 1 adds a focused downstream-sample-size sensitivity analysis, examining when pretrained representations help and how their residual error compares with Direct LR as more labels become available. v1 provides theoretical sample-complexity comparisons but no corresponding empirical analysis.

E5.justification: v2 adds basic repeated-run uncertainty reporting: Figure 1 specifies standard deviations over 10 runs, while Appendix D specifies three runs and Table 1 reports ± values. The table does not define its uncertainty statistic. v1 has no empirical run-count or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All empirical results are new. Figure 1 shows lower regression risk for pretrained representations at small sample sizes, but Direct LR overtakes them at large sizes as their risks plateau. Table 1 reports top-5 accuracies of 7.5 ± 0.3% for InfoNCE and 9.4 ± 0.1% for chi-squared learning. These are additions, not cross-version performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix B.3 replaces explicit conditions for extending Theorem 2 to other losses, including convexity in x-y and a relaxed triangle inequality, with a statement covering any semimetric convex in x for each y. This locally revises the stated loss assumptions; the numbered theoretical results and their central proofs remain intact.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about generalized approximate sufficiency, contrastive-loss minimization, and downstream performance controlled by sufficiency and augmentation error. The added experiments support these existing claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: Section 6 newly interprets regression error plateaus through encoder insufficiency and augmentation error. Appendix D qualifies the CLIP comparison as small-scale and compute-limited, notes possible effects of further tuning and larger datasets, and explicitly declines to claim chi-squared superiority. Existing theoretical limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial experimental implementation documentation: a two-layer ReLU encoder with hidden width 64 and Adam at learning rate 0.001, plus RN50-quickgelu CLIP, AdamW weight decay 0.02, loss-specific link functions, trainable temperature initialization, and the learning-rate search. These details were absent from v1; some settings, including synthetic augmentation noise sigma_1, remain unspecified.

R1.justification: Three references are added: Daunhawer et al. on multimodal identifiability, von Kügelgen et al. on content/style separation, and Sharma et al. on Conceptual Captions. The first two extend Section 2's citation coverage; the third documents the new dataset. The central positioning relative to OLCM25 remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammar and terminology corrections, adds an Experiments section and Appendix D, and updates the roadmap and contents. The conclusion becomes Section 7. The established narrative and organization of the theoretical development and proofs remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 1, an error-bar plot with three method curves and a logarithmic risk axis, and Table 1, a compact accuracy comparison. These are new displays rather than relocated content. The existing theoretical displays and overall single-column layout are retained, with accompanying pagination changes.

improvement.justification: v2 supplements the retained theoretical contribution with useful empirical evidence: Figure 1 illustrates the sample-efficiency tradeoff, and Appendix D demonstrates a limited real-data application with appropriately qualified claims. Repeated runs and implementation details improve assessability. The gain remains modest because the experiments are narrow, the synthetic augmentation-noise value is unspecified, and Table 1 leaves its uncertainty statistic undefined.
